title: Neighbours and chain distance from the witness angle

key_results.statement: For distinct points $x,x'\in X_V$: $x\asymp x'$ (related) iff $W(x,x')>0$, equivalently $\alpha(x,x')<\pi/2$; $\Gamma_V$ is the graph on $X_V$ whose edges are the related pairs.
For distinct points $x,x'\in X_V$: $x\asymp x'$ iff the view has a nonzero cross term $(V_A)_{hh'}\neq0$, for one, equivalently every, pair $h\in x$, $h'\in x'$.

Distinct points $x,x'$ are neighbours, $x\sim x'$, iff $x\asymp x'$ and no $y\in X_V$ satisfies $\max\bigl(\alpha(x,y),\alpha(y,x')\bigr)<\alpha(x,x')$; $N_V$ is the graph of neighbour pairs. The relation is symmetric and well defined in the sense of M6.

The relation $\sim$ is unchanged if $\alpha$ is replaced by $g\circ\alpha$ for any strictly increasing $g$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ (and $\alpha<\pi/2$ by $g\circ\alpha<g(\pi/2)$); in particular $x\sim x'$ iff $\cos\alpha(x,x')>0$ and no $y$ has $\min\bigl(\cos\alpha(x,y),\cos\alpha(y,x')\bigr)>\cos\alpha(x,x')$, and likewise with $W$ in place of $\cos\alpha$.
Two points are joined by a chain in $\Gamma_V$ iff they are joined by a chain in $N_V$; hence $N_V$ and $\Gamma_V$ have the same connected components.

For $x,x'$ in the same component of $\Gamma_V$: $\ell(x,x'):=\min\Bigl\{\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\alpha(y_j,y_{j+1}) : y_0=x,\ y_m=x',\ y_j\sim y_{j+1}\Bigr\}$; $\ell(x,x'):=+\infty$ between different components.
$\ell$ is an extended metric on $X_V$ (a metric on each component), $\ell\ge\alpha$, and $\ell(x,x')=\alpha(x,x')$ whenever $x\sim x'$.

Chain example ($n\ge2$ places $h_i$, blur width $m\ge1$): for every $m\ge1$ the $n$ points $x_i=[h_i]$ are distinct, $\cos\alpha(x_i,x_j)=\max(0,\,m-\lvert i-j\rvert)/m$, so $\alpha(x_i,x_j)=\arccos(1-\lvert i-j\rvert/m)$ for $\lvert i-j\rvert<m$ and $\pi/2$ otherwise.
Chain example: $x_i\asymp x_j$ iff $1\le\lvert i-j\rvert\le m-1$; $\Gamma_V$ is the band graph with these edges.
Chain example with $m=1$: no two points are related; $\Gamma_V=N_V$ has no edges, and $\ell(x_i,x_j)=0$ for $i=j$, $+\infty$ for $i\neq j$.
Chain example with $m\ge2$: $x_i\sim x_j$ iff $\lvert i-j\rvert=1$, so $N_V$ is the chain $x_1\sim x_2\sim\dots\sim x_n$.
Chain example with $n=3$, $m=2$: $\ell(x_1,x_3)=2\pi/3>\pi/2=\alpha(x_1,x_3)$, so $\ell$ can exceed $\pi/2$.

open_issues: Comparison with the expected result shows no discrepancy in the closed forms: the points x_i are distinct for every m ≥ 1, not only for m ≥ 2, and formula (4.13) holds only for m ≥ 2, since at m = 1 the chain distance is +∞ off the diagonal (4.11), not |i − j|π/2.

Definition (4.3) uses a strict inequality, so ties do not remove an edge (for example, if all distinct pairs have the same W > 0, then N_V is complete); whether this is the desired behaviour is a question about other neighbour rules, which is out of scope.
That ℓ is well defined in the sense of M6 was not asked; it follows as in Step 2, since ℓ is built from N_V and α only.

consistency_checks.check: Product state: X_V is a single point, Γ_V and N_V have no edges and ℓ is identically 0; the nonzero cross terms occur only between places of the same point, consistent with (4.2).
Chain example with m = 1 via the view: V_A is diagonal, so by (4.2) alone no two points are related and every component of Γ_V is a single point, in agreement with (4.11) and (4.5).
Chain example with m ≥ n: Γ_V is complete while N_V is still the chain (4.12); for n = m = 3, ℓ(x_1,x_3) = 2 arccos(2/3) ≈ 1.682 exceeds α(x_1,x_3) = arccos(1/3) ≈ 1.231, consistent with ℓ ≥ α.
